header.tag_why: The signer's side (Angela's store team) was weighing store rollout credibility: a live return at the till, who installs, and a retailer to call. We described the store side but never showed it, and we answered installs with a partner while Adyen brought people who had done store rollouts.

evidence.excerpt: The store couldn't see the online order, so staff were refunding to gift cards or telling people to mail it back.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: they'd just launched a loyalty program that was supposed to work everywhere and didn't, because store and web were two different customer records.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Their COO, Angela, apparently stood in a store on December 27th watching the returns queue.
evidence.label: opinion

trigger.insight: This evaluation started as a store-operations failure owned by the COO, not as a checkout or tech project. Yet we ran the deal through the CTO and won 'the web side', which was never the reason they were buying. The December 27th story is hearsay ('apparently'), but even as company lore it tells you whose pain this was.
trigger.messaging: For omnichannel retail deals, open with the buy-online-return-in-store failure and the split customer record (one return, one loyalty profile), not M1's global or currency framing or our online checkout.

evidence.excerpt: The CTO, Raj. He ran the RFP, he was my contact the whole way.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Angela.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: ...Probably Angela. Raj wanted us. I think. He told me he did.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Once. The kickoff.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Tom first named Raj, but his only basis was that Raj was his contact. Angela signed with Adyen, her team asked for the stores workshop, and Tom met her once. Raj's support for us rests only on Raj saying so. Being our contact did not make him the decider.
decider.messaging: Retail messaging needs a COO and store-ops track (rollout, returns at the till, one accountable vendor) that the champion can carry upward, not only CTO-facing web material.

evidence.excerpt: they came in with a retail team, people who'd done store rollouts, and they talked about one platform for the tills and the website, on one contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And they named retailers Angela knew.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Raj forwarded me a list of 14 questions and 11 of them were about stores.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: Per Raj, Adyen reframed the evaluation from web to stores, and the question list moved to stores (11 of 14). That was our weakest ground. Their 'one contract' pitch lands directly on Angela's fear of 'two vendors pointing at each other'. Our answer on installs, bringing in a partner, effectively proposed a second vendor. All of this is relayed by Raj; Tom wasn't there.
competitor.messaging: State plainly who is accountable for a till outage and a store install (one contract, one escalation path), and put named store-rollout people and peer retailers in front of the store team before the competitor does.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the online checkout demo. Their ecommerce lead loved it. The wallets, the one-click piece.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Online and in-store on one platform, the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's a diagram.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Then she asked how a return works. Step by step. At the till.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: M3 failed with the audience it was written for. The head of store operations read it as a claim with no proof and immediately asked for the operational walkthrough. When asked what he said, Tom answered only that he described it. Our checkout pitch won over the ecommerce lead, who was not the person signing.
message.messaging: Replace M3's 'the line has pretty much disappeared' with a step-by-step, shown-live flow: an online order returned at a store till, refunded to the original payment and credited to the same loyalty profile.

evidence.excerpt: They asked for a half day on stores. I brought our solutions engineer and me. They had six people from store operations.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: When Bev asked who does the installs, I said we'd bring in a partner. She wrote something down and didn't ask another question.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Right before that, honestly, we were ahead. Raj said so. We'd won the web side.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: Tom places the loss at the workshop, but the store-heavy question list had already arrived. 'Ahead' was Raj's view of the web side, not the store side's view. We sent two people, neither of whom had run a store rollout, to meet six store operators. The partner answer told Bev that installs would sit with someone else.
decided.messaging: Our store pitch must name who installs, who runs the rollout and who answers a Saturday till outage. M5's tiered response times does not answer 'who shows up'.

evidence.excerpt: can I talk to them?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we couldn't set up a call in time.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Then a rollout plan. Dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We described it. We never showed it.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: Every gap was a proof gap, not a feature claim: a reference they could call, a rollout plan and a live return. A written case study (M8) does not answer a COO who wants to talk to a peer, especially when the competitor named retailers she knew. The transcript doesn't say whether we could have shown the return live or simply didn't.
gaps.messaging: Back retail claims with callable store references and a template rollout plan (dates, installs, old-till decommissioning) ready before the stores workshop, not case-study PDFs.

evidence.excerpt: One system for the tills and the website.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I don't want two vendors pointing at each other.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: one customer, one basket.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We kept saying 'in-person payments' and 'point of sale.' They said 'the tills.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: The customer described the problem in store-floor terms (tills, one customer, one basket, one vendor). We answered in category jargon ('unified commerce', 'point of sale'). Angela's line is about accountability, not technology, and it was the frame the competitor's 'one contract' spoke to.
language.messaging: In retail decks, use 'one system for the tills and the website' and 'one customer, one basket' as headlines, and say 'tills' rather than 'in-person payments' or 'point of sale'.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj directly (or Angela in a loss debrief): who made the final decision, and did the store team's workshop findings decide it?

gaps.question: What did you say when Bev asked how a return works at the till?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and the solutions engineer: what exactly was described, and could the return flow have been demoed live?

gaps.question: Did Raj actually back us internally?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj what he argued for in the final decision and what objections he heard from Angela's team.

gaps.question: What was the deal size (ACV)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom for the proposed ACV from the final quote.

gaps.question: What did they use before (incumbent)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom or Raj which provider(s) ran the tills and the website before Adyen.

gaps.question: How did we answer 'who shows up when a till goes down on a Saturday'?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom for our written response to the 14-question list, especially the support and installs answers.

close.rep_takeaway: Your contact is not your decider. When the questions shift to stores and the COO's team asks for a workshop, that is the signer telling you what matters. Get in front of her, bring someone who has run a store rollout, and show the return at the till instead of describing it.
